<p class="sardine-eyebrow">DERAILED / MARINE LIFE / EXPERIMENT NO. 016</p>

# First, make a sardine.

<p class="sardine-lede">At Aquamarine Fukushima, thousands of Japanese sardines moved together like one enormous creature. Before trying to explain a school, let's build just one fish.</p>

<div class="sardine-intro">ONE FISH → MOVEMENT → A SCHOOL</div>


## 02 / An engine for movement

One fish, two independent systems. The **generator** creates a body. The **movement engine** updates where that body is and which way it faces. The renderer just draws the current state.

The engine runs the same tiny loop every frame:

**Choose a direction → limit the turn → move forward → draw.**

Try **Free swim** to watch small changes in direction accumulate into a path. Switch to **Follow target**, then tap anywhere in the tank or press **New destination**. The fish turns towards its goal without snapping instantly to it.

The speed is measured in pixels per second and updates use elapsed time, so the fish doesn't swim faster just because a display has more frames per second. The heading is measured in radians; the turning agility slider controls the maximum radians it can turn per second.

The dotted swim path reveals where the fish *travels*. Its body, though, is deliberately drawn as a **side-view illustration**: when it turns around, we mirror it left-to-right instead of rotating it upside down. We allow a little nose-up or nose-down pitch, while keeping the dorsal fin and eye on top. This is a small movement model, not a biological account of how a sardine swims.

## 03 / What if there were hundreds?

That is the next detour: **separation** (don't crowd), **alignment** (head the same way), and **cohesion** (stay near neighbours). Together, those local rules form a simplified model called *Boids*. They help us explore emergence, but they are not a complete explanation of real sardine behaviour.

<p class="sardine-outro">The first question isn't “Who leads the school?” It's “What does each fish do?”</p>
